On Thu, Aug 3, 2017 at 2:41 AM, Keith Lau <genw...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Dear NIMBLE team,
>
> Thanks so much for developing the NIMBLE. I indeed feel it improves a lot than before. That said, I got several questions along with the attached test files:
>
> 1. A minor question: why use compileNimble() twice?
>     Please see Line 65 and 72 in test.r file.
>

The first call to compileNimble compiles the model.  The second call compiles the MCMC, which must be in the same project as the model so that it can use the model's functions (defined internally).  It is possible to compile both in one call to compileNimble.  If so, the returned object will be a list of objects to call the compiled results.

> 2. Why use nimbleFunction() within BUGS is slower than coding it within BUGS?
>     In test.r, using Line 37 instead of Line 29-36 apparently made NIMBLE slow.

I assume you are referring to slower run-time, not slower model building and compilation.  I can speculate about several reasons you may be seeing a surprising speed comparison.  One key to thinking about what will be more efficient to is to think about what calculations need to be done to accomplish an MCMC update.  Put another way, one needs to think about the model's graph.  The NRMprob version makes each p[n, i, 1:point] a single (vector) node.  It's parents in the graph will include every alpha[1:CC, i] and every tau[1:CC, i].  Sometimes a situation like this can make unnecessary calculations occur, because they are built into the graph.  I am not sure in your example if that is the case.

There are also some ways you could write NRMprob more efficiently.  Using "init = FALSE" in "numeric" will lead to faster compiled code.  On the other hand, more core R features now work in compiling nimbleFunctions, so you could use simply
nu <- c(1, exp(alpha*t + tau)).

>
> 3. C_model$calculateWAIC(burnIn=4000) is extremely slow.
>     See Line 86.

We'll look at this.

>
> 4. Can sort() function be used for order constraint?
>     For example, t1 = a1 + b1 and t2 = c1 + d1. I need t1 >= t2.

Can you clarify?  Have you tried using dconstraint?

>
> 5. Will mixture model withough writing marginalization function be supported?

Yes.  But is there a specific context you want to ask about?  Generally mixture models are common in hierarchical models and they are common in BUGS/JAGS/NIMBLE code.

Perry

messages.subject: Dynamic index
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
Sorry for so a naïve question. I'm trying to fit a multistate capture-recapture model (see code and toy data) using the new characteristics of nimble (dynamic index). The problem appear in the lines:

      z[i,t] ~ dcat(ps[z[i,t-1], i, t-1, 1:3])
      y[i,t] ~ dcat(po[z[i,t], i, t-1, 1:3])

The error message is "multivariate parameters cannot be expressions..."
Is it necessary here to create a specific function to separate as deterministic variable and use that variable as the parameter?

Thank you,
Jose

# Multistate capture-recapture models based on the book "Bayesian population analysis using

# WinBUGS -a hierarchical perspective" by Marc Kéry & Michael Schaub  (2012, Academic Press)

setwd('C:/')

# Execute function

CH <- data.matrix(read.table("stateMS.txt", header=FALSE))

# Compute vector with occasion of first capture

get.first <- function(x) min(which(x!=0))

f <- apply(CH, 1, get.first)

# Recode CH matrix: note, a 0 is not allowed in WinBUGS!

# 1 = seen alive as juvenile, 2 = seen alive as adult, 3 = not seen

rCH <- CH  # Recoded CH

rCH[rCH==0] <- 3

library(nimble)

## define the model

code <- nimbleCode({

  #----------------------------------------

  # Parameters:

  # phi.juv: juvenile survival probability

  # phi.ad <http://phi.ad>: adult survival probability

  # p: recapture probability

  #----------------------------------------

  # States (S):

  # 1 alive as juvenile

  # 2 alive as adult

  # 3 dead

  # Observations (O):

  # 1 seen as juvenile

  # 2 seen as adult

  # 3 not seen

  #----------------------------------------

  # Priors and constraints

  for (t in 1:(n.occasions-1)){

    phi.juv[t] <- mean.phijuv

    phi.ad <http://phi.ad>[t] <- mean.phiad

    p[t] <- mean.p

  }

  mean.phijuv ~ dunif(0, 1)

  mean.phiad ~ dunif(0, 1)

  mean.p ~ dunif(0, 1)

  # Define state-transition and observation matrices

  for (i in 1:nind){

    # Define probabilities of state S(t+1) given S(t)

    for (t in f[i]:(n.occasions-1)){

      ps[1,i,t,1] <- 0

      ps[1,i,t,2] <- phi.juv[t]

      ps[1,i,t,3] <- 1-phi.juv[t]

      ps[2,i,t,1] <- 0

      ps[2,i,t,2] <- phi.ad <http://phi.ad>[t]

      ps[2,i,t,3] <- 1-phi.ad <http://1-phi.ad>[t]

      ps[3,i,t,1] <- 0

      ps[3,i,t,2] <- 0

      ps[3,i,t,3] <- 1

      # Define probabilities of O(t) given S(t)

      po[1,i,t,1] <- 0

      po[1,i,t,2] <- 0

      po[1,i,t,3] <- 1

      po[2,i,t,1] <- 0

      po[2,i,t,2] <- p[t]

      po[2,i,t,3] <- 1-p[t]

      po[3,i,t,1] <- 0

      po[3,i,t,2] <- 0

      po[3,i,t,3] <- 1

    } #t

  } #i

  # State-space model likelihood

  for (i in 1:nind){

    z[i,f[i]] <- y[i,f[i]]

    for (t in (f[i]+1):n.occasions){

      # State equation: draw S(t) given S(t-1)

      z[i,t] ~ dcat(ps[z[i,t-1], i, t-1, 1:3])

      # Observation equation: draw O(t) given S(t)

      y[i,t] ~ dcat(po[z[i,t], i, t-1, 1:3])

    } #t

  } #i

})

# Bundle data

data <- list(y = rCH)

constants<-list(f = f, n.occasions = dim(rCH)[2], nind = dim(rCH)[1])

# Initial values

age.ms.init <- function(ch){

  init <- ch

  al <- which(ch==2, arr.ind = T)

  for (i in 1:nrow(al)){

    init[al[i,1], f[al[i,1]]:al[i,2]] <- 2

  }

  for (i in 1:nrow(init)){

    init[i,1:f[i]] <- NA

  }

  return(init)

}

inits <- list(mean.phijuv = runif(1, 0, 1), mean.phiad = runif(1, 0, 1),

  mean.p = runif(1, 0, 1), z = age.ms.init(rCH))

nimbleOptions(showCompilerOutput = TRUE)

nimbleOptions(allowDynamicIndexing = TRUE)

Rmodel <- nimbleModel(code=code, constants=constants, data=data, inits=inits)

Cmodel <- compileNimble(Rmodel)

rCH[rCH==0] <- 3

  #----------------------------------------

  # Parameters:

  # phi.juv: juvenile survival probability

  # 2 seen as adult

  mean.p ~ dunif(0, 1)

      ps[1,i,t,3] <- 1-phi.juv[t]

      ps[3,i,t,1] <- 0

      ps[3,i,t,2] <- 0

      ps[3,i,t,3] <- 1

      po[1,i,t,1] <- 0

      po[1,i,t,2] <- 0

      po[1,i,t,3] <- 1

      po[2,i,t,1] <- 0

      po[2,i,t,2] <- p[t]

      po[2,i,t,3] <- 1-p[t]

      po[3,i,t,1] <- 0

      po[3,i,t,2] <- 0

      po[3,i,t,3] <- 1

    } #t

  } #i

  for (i in 1:nind){

    z[i,f[i]] <- y[i,f[i]]

    for (t in (f[i]+1):n.occasions){

      # State equation: draw S(t) given S(t-1)

      z[i,t] ~ dcat(ps[z[i,t-1], i, t-1, 1:3])

      # Observation equation: draw O(t) given S(t)

      y[i,t] ~ dcat(po[z[i,t], i, t-1, 1:3])

library(nimble)

## Let me give a simpler worked example.
## Say we have a function in R that will only work in R.  This is like the function nearPD in your case.
## I will make the function take a few inputs and return a list, of which we really only want one element.
## We can't use this directly because some inputs and its output are not amenable to the nimble compiler
doSomethingInR <- function(x, ## some input of interest, expected to be a numeric vector
                           y, ## another input of interest, expected to a numeric vector
                           label, ## input NOT of interest, expected for example to be a character vector
                           v = 0 ## input NOT of interest, but with an acceptable default value
                           ) {
    answer <- x^2 + y^2 + v## something we'll pretend you can only do in R
    additionalInformation <- sum(x * y)  ## some other step that you don't care about.
    if(label == "Whatever") print("So what?") ## some use of the argument you don't care about
    return(list(answer = answer, also = additionalInformation)) ## information happens to be returned in a list -- not useable in a nimbleModel or nimbleFunction
}

## Next I make a wrapper to doSomethingInR that has inputs and outputs amenable to nimble
wrapDoSomethingInR <- function(x, y) { ## take only the numeric inputs
    result <- doSomethingInR(x, y, label = "I just need to provide this to make doSomethingInR happy.") ## default for v is ok
    result$answer  ## return only the numeric input
}

## Next I create a nimbleFunction that calls wrapDoSomethingInR, since it has allowed input and output types.
nimbleDoSomethingInR <- nimbleRcall(function(x = double(1), y = double(1)) {},
                                    returnType = double(1),
                                    'wrapDoSomethingInR')

## Now we can use nimbleDoSomethingInR in nimbleModel or a nimbleFunction
## A couple of bumps in this experimental feature: we must we calculate = FALSE in nimbleModel.  And we can only use the model after compiling it.

model <- nimbleModel(
    nimbleCode({
        for(i in 1:10) x[i] ~ dnorm(1,1)
        for(i in 1:10) y[i] ~ dnorm(-1,1)
        z2[1:10] <- nimbleDoSomethingInR(x[1:10], y[1:10])
        }), calculate = FALSE) ## Currently we need calculate = FALSE here to avoid a warning

## The model will not run in uncompiled mode.  It must be compiled.

cmodel <- compileNimble(model)
## Let's verify if it works:
cmodel$simulate()
cmodel$x
cmodel$y
cmodel$z2
cmodel$x^2 + cmodel$y^2 ## these values should match cmodel$z2

Dear Ugoline,

Are you trying to make this work via nimbleRcall or via turning nearPD into a nimbleFunction?

If you want to make it work via nimbleRcall, please see my previous message and email me directly if it is not clear.  We can later post a message to the group highlighting any useful clarifications that come up.

If you want to turn it into a nimbleFunction, Fritz has made a good start fixing it for you.  The R functions that are supported for compilation in nimbleFunctions are listed in several tables in Chapter 10 of the user manual.  You’ll see that none of the functions identified in the warning message are supported.  Therefore for trcrossprod and norm, you’ll have to replace them with linear algebra expressions.  Instead of creating an R list using structure(), you’ll have to define a nimbleList type and then return a nimbleList of that type (User Manual Chapter 13.2).  However, if you want to use the function directly in a BUGS model, it must return a numeric object, not a nimbleList, because nimbleLists are not part of models.   Please feel free to email me directly if the list of supported functions in Chapter 10, or the system for declaring argument and return types (Chapter 10.4), are not clear or if you have other questions.  Again if we reach a solution we can then share it on the list for the benefit of others.

The user manual is here: https://r-nimble.org/manuals/NimbleUserManual.pdf

Thanks
Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ugoline,

Below is a demo for using the nimbleRcall approach for using nearPD within a nimbleModel.  I hope this works.  Let us know further questions.

Perry

## Demo of wrapping Matrix::nearPD for use in a compiled nimbleModel
library(Matrix)
library(nimble)
## Be sure not to source your copy of nearPD.  Having a copy in .GlobalEnv
## doesn't seem to work, because it needs to find other functions in
## the Matrix package namespace.  Just rely on R's finding it from the
## Matrix package.

## Wrap to simplify arguments and return type. It looks like in the
## case of nearPD, the element you want is not named "answer" (as
## in the general example I made previously) but rather "mat".
WrapNearPD <- function (x,eig.tol = 1e-06, conv.tol = 1e-07, posd.tol = 1e-08, maxit = 100){
  result<-nearPD(x,eig.tol = 1e-06, conv.tol = 1e-07, posd.tol = 1e-08, maxit = 100)
  as.matrix(result$mat) ## The result needs to be converted to a plain
                                     ## R matrix, not a dpoMatrix of package Matrix.
}

## Make the nimbleRcall: It looks like in the case of nearPD, the
## input is a matrix (2D double) "x", and there is no "y" that I can
## see (again perhaps these were leftover from the general example
## I had provided previously), so I've modified the argument type
## declarations for NIMBLE.
## It also looks like the returnType should be 2D.
nimbleNearPD <- nimbleRcall(function(x = double(2)) {},
                                    returnType = double(2),
                                    'WrapNearPD')

## Finally, try using it in a model:
testModelCode <- nimbleCode({
    xNearPD[1:5, 1:5] <- nimbleNearPD(x[1:5, 1:5])
})

testModel <- nimbleModel(testModelCode, check = FALSE, calculate = FALSE)
## note that a model with a nimbleRcall will only work compiled (a
## loose end that is one reason we marked it as an "experimental"
## feature).

ctestModel <- compileNimble(testModel)

## Let's see if it works:
ctestModel$x <- matrix(rnorm(25), nrow = 5)

## Answer directly from nearPD:
nearPD(ctestModel$x)$mat
## Answer via the nimble model:
ctestModel$calculate('xNearPD[1:5, 1:5]')
ctestModel$xNearPD  #This result should match the answer calculated directly from nearPD.

messages.subject_clean: proposal to add control parameters in MCMC samplers
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

we have uncountered some difficulties in reaching convergence of models with basic MCMC samplers - namely RW & RW_block.

We seem to have found out some possibilities to resolve these by controlling the parameters of the sampler - especially the scale parameter. However, it would be smarter for us to have extra parameters to control the MCMC sampler and ask whether this hould be possible to add them in future versions of Nimble. These parameters could concer RW & RW-block sampers but maybe also other ones. I suggest two parameters: (teh names of the parameters are juste suggestions)

nadaptPN: number of initial MCMC iterations (prior to thinning) during which the statistical parameter(s) is (are) not adapted.

nadaptSN: number of initial MCMC iterations (prior to thinning) during which the scale parameter(s) used to adapt the statistical parameter(s) is (are) not adapted.

Sincerely,

Frédéric Gosselin
Irstea
Nogent-sur-Vernisson
France

Frédéric, I'm very happy to hear about your interest in NIMBLE.  Thanks for the ideas and suggestions.  We'll discuss the possibility of including these options in NIMBLE's samplers, but in the meantime, it is very straightforward to write your own sampler implementing these options.  Then, the new sampler can immediately be used in the MCMC.

I'm happy to help write this, no problem at all.  First, let me make sure I understand what you're looking for:

nadaptPN.  I'm not entirely sure what you mean by "statistical parameter(s) is (are) not adapted."  Do you mean fFor this many (pre-thinning) iterations, do you mean the sampler would not update the variable in the statistical model? -- meaning, the sampler would do nothing, for the first nadaptPN iterations?

nadaptSN.  This one, I believe I understand.  I think you're saying the scale parameter (or in the case of RW_block, both the scale and proposal covariance) parameters, which are used for the M-H update of the model variables, are not adapted.  Hence, these would stay fixed at their initial values (scale = 1, and proposal covariance = identity matrix, unless you specify them to begin at some other values) for the first nadaptSN MCMC iterations.  Is that correct?

Cheers,
Daniel
